- Sebastian Klovig Skelton, Data & ethics editor

Amazon is using an artificial intelligence (AI) powered risk-scoring system that combines “hundreds of data points” to track union activity amongst its workforce globally, leaked documents reveal.

Disclosed as part of a labour dispute between Amazon and Canadian union Unifor – in which the British Columbia Labour Board ruled the e-commerce giant had violated multiple local labour laws – the internal documents reveal the company’s use of an AI-powered tool named Atlas to assess the risk of union organising at specific workplaces, as well as to predict where future unionisation efforts may emerge.

The documents specifically highlight how Atlas combines “hundreds of data points” collected from workers and their workplace environments, which are then used by Amazon to granularly measure the level of worker unrest per worksite.

Described in the documents as “a labor risk framework to clarify how Amazon evaluates emerging workforce issues, labor union targets, and internal or external labor threats”, the prediction model breaks Amazon sites into five tiers, with Tier 5 applied to facilities where there is “no immediate perceived risk” and Tier 1 applied where “future activity is imminent”.

While the documents largely focus on the Canadian context, they show that Atlas surveillance is being conducted in the UK, with two warehouse sites – BHX4 in Coventry and EMA4 in Minworth – included in Amazon’s list of Tier 1 sites and described as “risky”.

The Coventry site was previously involved in a wave of unofficial wildcat strikes that struck the e-commerce giant in August 2022 , in which hundreds of workers across the country independently staged walkouts, sit-ins and work slowdowns in protest of derisory pay rises.

Following the disclosure, the GMB Union has accused Amazon of “Orwellian” behaviour towards its workers, urging it to come clean on exactly how it monitors union activity among its workforce. It has also called on the government to urgently seek answers from Amazon about its use of Atlas in British workplaces.

“This is a shocking revelation,” said GMB organiser Rachel Fagan. “Amazon, one of the globe’s wealthiest corporations, could be deploying Orwellian AI-fuelled tools to monitor workers right here in the UK. We’ve long warned that Amazon top brass is uninterested in the norms and expectations of British industrial relations.”

> This is a shocking revelation. Amazon, one of the globe’s wealthiest corporations, could be deploying Orwellian AI-fuelled tools to monitor workers right here in the UK Rachel Fagan, GMB Union

As a result, GMB has written to the UK’s minister for the future of work, Kate Dearden, and Liam Byrne, chair of the UK’s Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, to demand urgent answers about the situation.

GMB further highlighted that Amazon’s practices have been revealed just weeks before new access rights come into effect for trade unions in the UK, giving them the right to visit and communicate with staff in the workplace.

“Workers deserve to be able to work free of the fear of excessive surveillance,” said Fagan. “If Amazon bosses are using Atlas or similar AI-fuelled systems in the UK, the British public deserve to know.”

Rosa Curling, co-executive director at Foxglove, added: “It is shocking that Amazon think they can deploy a nakedly anti-union spy tech tool for the purpose of disrupting workers’ legal rights to organise and form a union.”

She said that Foxglove is urgently considering this new development with the warehouse workers and their lawyers, who are already suing Amazon over its allegedly “unlawful” use of “one-click-to-quit” QR codes that, if scanned by workers, automatically generate and send emails to their trade union ending their membership.

Foxglove added it is concerned the software may be breaching the right of employees to organise and join a union.

Under UK data protection rules , excessive, routine, or unnecessarily intrusive monitoring can constitute a breach of the law. Trade union membership and activity also count as “special category data”, placing further restrictions on how it can be used.

Computer Weekly contacted Amazon about its use of Atlas, as well as the claims made by Foxglove and the GMB.

In response, a spokesperson said Atlas is not used for individual employee monitoring or surveillance, and that no personal data is collected from workers. They added that the data collected by Atlas is aggregated to measure sentiment at the work site level only, to identify where a site needs more support.

The spokesperson concluded it was inaccurate to suggest the company is using AI algorithms to monitor union activity, and completely wrong to reference surveillance of employees.

> The GMB’s characterisation is wrong. This isn’t surveillance. Like any responsible employer, we have numerous ways for our team to provide us with feedback, and we use that feedback to identify where we can improve the day-to-day experience of our employees Amazon spokesperson

“The GMB’s characterisation is wrong. This isn’t surveillance,” said an Amazon spokesperson. “Like any responsible employer, we have numerous ways for our team to provide us with feedback, and we use that feedback to identify where we can improve the day-to-day experience of our employees.”

Computer Weekly contacted GMB for a copy of the letter sent to British politicians, but received no response.

## Workforce surveillance

The data collected by the company includes the number of employee trainings completed, health and safety incidents, workers’ feedback on management, worker tenure and turnover, local minimum wage rates, the number of appeals or investigations at a site, and a variety of other data.

Other information considered is the proximity of warehouses to other warehouses with union activity.

Included in Amazon’s Tier 1 list, for example, is its LDJ5 warehouse in Staten Island, New York. This site sits directly opposite its JFK8 warehouse, which was the first Amazon facility to unionise in April 2022 following a multi-year organising battle against the company.

Another key source of data for the Atlas tool comes from monitoring forums where workers communicate. This includes internal communication channels, such as the company’s Voice of the Associate (VOA) electronic bulletin board, and external channels like Reddit.

According to the documents, using AI to identify phrases and “common keywords” enables managers to do a “deep dive into the worker population driving the discussion”.

Amazon also tracks and documents all organising activities detected by managers and records them under the category of “employee relations events”.

Each activity is then assigned a severity score, with events like employees signing union cards, delegations of workers approaching management with demands, protests, sickouts and work stoppages being marked as “high severity”.

## ‘Employee Relations 101’

The internal documents also contain training materials for Amazon’s Canadian managers, which can help them spot “employee relations events” for inclusion in Atlas.

Titled Employee Relations 101, the materials set out how “leaders” should approach employees in a range of situations and circumstances, including to stave off what Amazon views as the threat of unionisation.

“Overall, a union coming into your site could fundamentally change the way it operates today. It would likely add layers of bureaucracy and jeopardize your ability to make changes to improve the workplace for employees as well as improve the end customer experience,” one document states.

“It is important then for you to recognize and escalate labor activity concerns quickly. This will help ensure we are doing all we can to build trust, minimize disruptions, and maintain safe operations.”

Elsewhere in the documents, Amazon adds: “Whether internally started or externally started – strategy of unions is like strategy of someone splitting wood. Look for a crack and put a wedge there to drive separation between management and employees.”

> Strategy of unions is like strategy of someone splitting wood. Look for a crack and put a wedge there to drive separation between management and employees Amazon manager training document

Amazon then goes on to highlight a range of indicators that could signal possible union activity, urging managers to get in touch with its HR and employee relations departments if they, for example, notice an abnormal increase in absenteeism, or groups of employees start asking increasingly hostile questions about company benefits and policies.

It also highlights employees starting to use expressions related to labour discussions, including “grievance”, “just cause”, “living wage”, or “seniority” as something to watch out for, or using phrases common in labour organising like “we” and “on behalf of”.

It added that other signs of “escalating labor activity” include third-party flyers, anti-Amazon or union graffiti, and lists of demands circulating where people raise concerns on behalf of co-workers.

The presentation also trains managers on how to deal with employees in ways that do not violate their labour rights when signs of union activity are spotted.

Using the acronym “FORE”, it notes that managers “can have open, two-way conversations that avoid violating employee rights by focusing on sharing facts, opinions, rules and experiences”.

This section adds that while “you can always remind employees of the benefits they have as an employee with Amazon” – including competitive pay, a “comprehensive” benefits package and career growth opportunities – “sharing negative opinions and experiences about unions [or unionisation] is a high-risk activity … [because it] is not permitted employer speech” in certain Canadian provinces.

In terms of VOA use – one of the key communication channels that feeds into Amazon’s Atlas system – it advises managers not to use security cameras to determine who wrote a comment on the electronic bulletin, and specifically says “do not discipline employees for VOA comments without approval from Legal”.

The document goes on to instruct managers to follow another acronym, TIPS, which reminds them to never “threaten, interrogate, promise or spy”.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s request for comment on why it sees workers organising as a threat to its business, an Amazon spokesperson said its employees always have the option of joining a union or not, and that what matters most to the company is the direct relationships between workers and managers.

They added that any mention of maintaining operations or minimising disruption made in the documents refers to when there is industrial action, should it happen.

An Amazon spokesperson informed Computer Weekly that the system referred to in the documents is no longer called Atlas, but declined to divulge what the system is currently named.

In April 2020, Computer Weekly reported that Amazon-owned Whole Foods was using an interactive “heat-mapping” tool to track dozens of metrics – such as employee turnover, diversity and proximity to union offices – to predict and mitigate unionisation risks at its 510 US stores.
